# Brainstorm of the Metis front-end rewritten from scratch

Decision log of the brainstorm that began on 05/10/2026, following the format of
`spec/backend-brainstorm-log.md`. Every question sent to the product owner, the answer
given verbatim and the assumptions in use are all recorded here, so that the new spec is written from it. When the
new spec is done, this log is its record.

## 1. Context

- The code of the previous attempt was abandoned and deleted on 05/10/2026: `apps/`, `packages/`,
  `tools/`, the build, test and lint configuration, and the automated check pipeline. Decision `N-10` in
  spec version 04/10 section 16.1; the list of every file is in
  `.superpowers/sdd/2026-10-04-frontend-foundation/progress.md`.
- Spec version 04/10 and plan version 04/10 are now only records. The repo has only the inputs and the documentation left.
- Spec written from this log: `spec/2026-10-05-frontend-foundation-spec.md` (awaiting approval, FE-16).
  The spec amends two places of the log: rule 2 in section 7.3 (screens of V2 and V3 carry the Planned label even though they have a
  wireframe, exactly as in the wireframe's sidebar) and section 8.6 (a token generator is still needed, because
  React Native cannot read CSS variables).

## 2. Assumptions in use

Sent to the product owner on 05/10/2026, not yet corrected.

1. The goal stays the same: a screen counts as done only when the machine can prove it through six
   gates (token, visual, behavior, translation, brand, accessibility); build exactly one
   screen to sign off, and only then replicate.
2. The acceptance screen is `24-project-overview`.
3. The technology stack and the versions pinned in spec version 04/10 section 3 are still used, installed fresh. The six
   root causes in spec version 04/10 section 2 all lie in how the work and the checking were done, not
   in the technology stack.
4. Inputs: BRD version 4.5, `wireframes/`, `brand/`, the defect log
   `analysis/metis-storefront/evidences/2026-10-04-so-loi.md`.
5. The six front-end contracts that the back-end session treats as locked
   (`spec/backend-brainstorm-log.md` line 17) are kept, because they are designs on paper
   and not code. In the first batch they define the shape of the mock data.

- BRD version 4.5 line 1186: the Delayed metric shows "not baselined" before CHG-06.

  the source record. The sentence "the interface does not compute metrics itself" of the old spec is an inference

  The first batch builds no back-end (FE-05). On 05/10/2026 the product owner reopened `BD-01`

- Wireframe of screen 24 (`wireframes/screens/24-project-overview.html` lines 16 and 39):
  the project Meridian CGI Campaign of Northwind Furniture Co., progress 25%.
- The tools still in the repo are self-contained: `brand/tools` and `wireframes/tools` have their own
  `package.json`; `brd/source` uses standard Python.
- BRD version 4.5 line 1643 (D-19): a responsive web version for Focus, Board, Overview and
  approvals; the overview screen must run on a phone.
- BRD version 4.5 line 694 (PLT-04): a missing permission must be explained and never
  shown as a blank page: no permission (with an action to request permission), read-only, session expired.
- BRD version 4.5 line 704 (PLT-14): export a project or workspace to a JSON data file.
  No requirement was found that names the Share button of the project header.
- Fonts: Google Fonts lists the `cyrillic-ext` character set before `latin` for Inter and Manrope,
  so taking the first file takes the wrong character set; one must take them by the name of the `latin` and

  section 8), while `brand/style-guide.html` line 8 loads `opsz,wght@6..72,500`.
- Safari 27 on the Mac (05/10/2026): the product owner confirmed that "Show features for web
  developers" and "Allow remote automation and external agents" were already on ("these 2 were already
  on"). An automation session is rejected when Safari is open by hand (system log: `Rejecting
  session ...: Safari was not launched for automation`), and it runs within 3 seconds when Safari
  is closed. In Xcode 27, the Simulator lives in the DeviceHub app.

## 6. Design, part 1: architecture and data (approved, FE-06)

1. **Front-end only, the mock server answers.** No real server, no metrics calculation
   engine. The screen calls the API exactly as it would with a real server; the MSW mock server (Mock
   Service Worker, a library that returns prepared data for API calls, both in the
   browser and in tests, as spec version 04/10 section 11 chose) answers instead. When
   the back-end exists, the mock server is turned off, with no change to the screens.
2. **Hand-written mock data**, following the wireframe of screen 24 and BRD section 12: the project Meridian
   CGI Campaign of Northwind Furniture Co. Each number is a snapshot made of a value,
   the timestamp of the data and the version of the metric definition (BR-39), with a filter to
   drill down (BR-32). The screen never counts or adds up any row, it only shows what the snapshot
   says (MCP-10: the numbers are computed by the platform). The test "25 percent, not 22"
   therefore checks that the screen shows exactly the snapshot; the rule of not counting Category nodes
   (BR-24) belongs to the back-end.
3. **The API contract written in zod** (a library that checks the shape of data). The app checks every
   API response against this contract at run time, so data of the wrong shape shows up as
   a clear error rather than a silently wrong screen. When the back-end starts, this contract is
   what gets handed over.
4. **A single app `apps/web`**, no multi-package workspace, no path aliases. The
   folder name is the same as last time but the code is written completely anew. The design system is the folder
   `apps/web/src/design-system/`; a lint rule forbids it from importing the rest of the app, and
   all of its displayed text goes through a required prop (`N-06`). Reason: last time the CSS of
   the design system sat outside the app root, so Tailwind scanned the wrong place and lost the layout classes
   (spec version 04/10 section 12: turning off the two source-declaration lines makes the `h-9` class come out as 0 pixels). Split
   packages when there is a second place of use, for example the server.

### 7.3 Controls leading to screens not yet built

The first batch has only one screen, so nearly every navigation item, every tab and every drill
down (OVW-04) leads to a screen that does not exist yet. Three rules:

1. The target is one of the 58 screens: a real link with the final path. That path
   opens a common page "not built in the first batch" inside the real shell, stating the name of the target screen
   and the requirement ids taken from `wireframes/manifest.json`, the path of the wireframe file, and the
   filter received. When the target screen is built, the common page is replaced and the overview screen is not
   changed. Example: clicking the Blocked tile opens WBS with `status=blocked`.
2. A feature with no screen among the 58 screens: the label "Planned V2" or "Planned V3"
   per style guide section 6 (Investment, Scenarios, SteerCo, AI copilot; the help button
   and the glossary of PLT-20).
3. A control whose target screen is unclear: Share (no named requirement) and Export (leaning
   toward PLT-14, which belongs to screen `44-data-export-delete`). Record it in the open questions of the spec; for now
   follow rule 1 if a screen can be identified, otherwise it is plain text with the label "Not built yet".

Change from spec version 04/10 (`N-04`): the old rule gave every control without a screen the
label Planned V2; the new rule uses the label only for a feature with no screen among the 58
screens, because the first batch has only one screen.

### 7.4 Three width levels (style guide section 5.1, BRD D-19)

- From 1280 px: full. 768 to 1279 px: the sidebar shrinks to an icon column. Below 768
  px: one column, 44 x 44 px touch targets.
- Further proposal, not drawn in the wireframe: below 768 px, a menu button in the top bar opens the
  sidebar as a sliding drawer.

### 7.5 States

Loading; no permission (an explanation and the Request access button, PLT-04); session expired
(a sign-in-again dialog); read-only (a banner strip with the reason); no baseline yet; stale
or missing data (freshness "Stale", "Partial"); an empty list with a sentence on why it is empty. Viewable
in the app through three projects of the tree: Meridian CGI Campaign with full data, Northwind Showroom
VR with no baseline and stale data, Spring Catalogue Renders with no permission. Every
state is also in Storybook.

## 8. Design, part 3: the translation layer, six gates, reverse tests (approved, FE-08)

### 8.1 The translation layer

- Each screen and shell has its own strings folder: `strings/en.ts` is the original,
  `strings/vi.ts` must have exactly every key of the original, and TypeScript catches that at
  compile time: a missing Vietnamese key is a compile error. Dictionaries are not merged between
  screens, so there is no room for two screens to translate one key two ways (the 31-key bug, spec version
  04/10 section 8.2). English sentences are not used as keys and objects are not wrapped in a proxy,
  so the bug of text inside arrays and nested objects going untranslated is gone.
- Data from the API carries only codes and user content (project names, item names, names of
  people). The labels of the codes (status, type, risk level) live in the strings of the screen. User
  content is not translated.
- Dates, times, numbers and percentages are formatted per language with the browser's `Intl`.
- The language picker is the `Select` of React Aria Components in the top bar, showing the names in the
  native language "English", "Tieng Viet"; English is the default. The choice is stored in the browser
  (the first batch has no real accounts yet); the `lang` attribute of the page is set before the first
  paint; changing the language changes the text of the screen at once, without reloading the page.
- Adding a language: add a strings file next to each `en.ts` and one line in the
  list of languages; no component is edited.
- Components of the design system receive all text through a required prop, with no default text
  (`N-06`).
- The Vietnamese version is drafted by whoever writes the code, and the product owner reviews it when reviewing the screen.

### 8.2 The six gates of the acceptance screen

| Gate | What it measures | How it is measured |
|---|---|---|
| Token | No visual number is hard-coded in `apps/web/src` | A script scans for arbitrary-value classes, hex color codes and pixel numbers; only the two exceptions of spec version 04/10 section 5.3, each with a comment giving the reason; state variants such as `aria-[current=page]:` are not counted. A test requires every needed token to become a utility class with exactly one mapping in the theme, with three groups deliberately having no mapping (focus ring, status colors, chart colors) |
| Shape | The rendered DOM tree matches the numbers in `brand/tokens.css` | Playwright reads `brand/tokens.css` directly and then measures: sidebar 232, top bar 52, page margin 24, list rows from 44, metric tile number size 28, Newsreader title 30, corner radii 6 and 8; at the three width levels, no horizontal scrolling |
| Behavior | Every control does what the screen contract declares | The screen contract (a file declaring each control of the screen and what it does: go to a path, write a filter into the path, open a dialog, change a state). The test reads the contract directly at run time, clicks each control, measures the effect; the reverse check requires every control in the content area to be present in the contract; every link of the shell opens a page that has a title; the browser console has no errors |
| Translation | After switching to Vietnamese, no English interface text remains | A type check catches missing keys; a test requires the variables in a sentence to match the original and no Vietnamese sentence to be identical to the English one except for an approved list of loanwords; in the browser, no sentence of `en.ts` is still shown after the switch, `lang` is correct, the choice survives a reload, the layout does not break |
| Brand | Real fonts and the real logo | Three typefaces self-contained in the repo, taken by the name of the `latin` and `vietnamese` blocks; Newsreader taken at exactly the optical size range that the style guide loads (measure again when building); the browser reports them loaded and the computed `font-family` matches the token; the logo is an image pointing at the byte-for-byte copy of `brand/logo`; the favicon and app icon load |
| Accessibility | No severe errors, usable by keyboard and by finger | axe-core (a tool that scans for accessibility errors) finds no errors of serious or critical level in every state; touch targets on a phone from 44 x 44; every control is reachable with the Tab key and has a focus ring |

Runs on four platforms: Chromium, WebKit, Firefox, Pixel 7.

### 8.3 Reverse tests

Each gate has a deliberate breakage that proves it knows how to report red:

| Breakage | Gate that must go red |
|---|---|
| Add an arbitrary-value class to a component | Token |
| Change a number in `brand/tokens.css` without changing the code | Shape |
| Remove the path of a navigation item | Behavior |
| Add a button not declared in the screen contract | Reverse check |
| Delete a Vietnamese sentence | Translation |
| Change the logo into text | Brand |
| Shrink a button below 44 pixels | Accessibility |

A script breaks the code, runs the gate, demands red, then restores the original state whatever the result. The
reverse tests run separately, not inside the unit test suite, because they need a browser (the lesson
of the unfinished run on 05/10).

### 8.4 The test framework

Vitest with jsdom for components and logic; Playwright for the four platforms; MSW supplies mock
data to both; Storybook for each component and each state of the screen, with
axe-core. The automated check pipeline on GitHub Actions: one job for the type check, lint and
unit tests; one job for Playwright.

### 8.5 Conditions to sign off the first screen

Six gates green on four platforms; the seven reverse tests all red at exactly the right gate; the product owner views
the real screen in two languages, at three width levels, through every state, then signs off. After
sign-off, the screenshots of the screen at each width level become the reference images; from then on a visual change not
intended is red.

### 8.6 Changes from spec version 04/10

- Drop the theme generator (section 5.2): a hand-written mapping plus a test for all tokens, less code and
  still no way to miss a token.
- Drop the generator of four test files (section 10): the test reads the screen contract directly at run time,
  so there is no generated file to drift out of sync.
- Drop the gate that reads the built CSS (section 5.4): the CSS now lives in the app, and measuring the DOM tree is
  enough to catch a missing class.
- Drop the proxy-style translation layer and the merging of dictionaries (section 8.2): each screen has its own typed dictionary.

## 9. New requirement: bring it to the Android and iOS mobile apps later, with the least effort (awaiting a choice, FE-09)

> This section is the first proposal draft. The product owner afterwards demanded one codebase for every platform, reopened
> the back-end language (FE-10) and set a performance condition on every device (FE-11).
> The evaluation table of the alternatives is in `spec/2026-10-05-cross-platform-research.md`.

The product owner's words, 05/10/2026: "we need to design it so that it can be put onto a
mobile app (Android and IOS) easily later and with the least effort".

Context: BRD version 4.5 line 1643 (D-19) fixes a responsive web version for Focus, Board,
Overview and approvals, with no native app in the MVP. This requirement does not contradict D-19:
it demands that today's design be ready for a mobile app later.

Sources checked on 05/10/2026:
- Capacitor: "a cross-platform native runtime that makes it easy to build performant
  mobile applications that run natively on iOS, Android"; "can be dropped into any
  existing modern JavaScript project"; device functions go through plugins; the current version
  is 8. [Source: https://capacitorjs.com/docs]
- Apple App Review section 4.2: "Your app should include features, content, and UI that
  elevate it beyond a repackaged website." [Source: https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/]

### 9.1 Three approaches

| Approach | Effort later | Change needed now | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wrap the web app itself with Capacitor (recommended) | Small: add the iOS and Android projects, connect plugins for secure storage, push notifications and files; submit to the stores. The screens stay unchanged | Small: the seams in section 9.2 | It feels more like a web app than a native one; Apple section 4.2 demands an app that is more than a packaged web page. Metis has real functionality so it will probably pass [Unverified - only known for sure when submitted] |
| A separate React Native app, sharing the part that is not interface | Large: rebuild the interface of every mobile screen with native components | Small: as in section 9.2 | Two interface layers must be kept in step with each other |
| Write the interface once for web and mobile with React Native for Web | Smallest per screen | Large: drop Tailwind and React Aria Components, change how every component is built | The author's assessment, not verified: Metis's tree tables, canvases and dense tables are hard to build and hard to make accessible on this platform; slow in the first batch |

### 9.2 Seams added to the approved design, if the Capacitor approach is chosen

1. A folder `apps/web/src/core/` for everything that is not interface: API calls, the zod
   contract, dictionaries, formatting, and the display logic of each screen (pure functions turning API
   data into what the screen shows). A lint rule forbids `core/` from importing React DOM, the design system
   or browser objects. If React Native is needed later, `core/` is reused as it is.
2. A folder `apps/web/src/platform/` wraps each platform-dependent thing: storage, the API address,
   file download, opening external links. One file for each; when moving to Capacitor only the inner part
   of that file is replaced with a plugin.
3. The API address comes from configuration and is an absolute address. [Unverified: in a Capacitor
   app, the page runs from a local origin, so a relative API path does not reach
   the server]
4. The phone layout is the main layout of the mobile app: leave the safe areas for the notch
   and the navigation bar, nothing shows only on hover, the sidebar opens as a sliding drawer.
5. Add an iPhone platform to Playwright, making it five platforms, so that the phone gate runs on both
   WebKit and Chromium.
6. The paths of the screens are kept stable, so that links opening straight into a screen in the app can be made later.

## 10. Design, part 4: the testing system and the leanness of the code (awaiting approval, FE-13)

Tool sources, read on 05/10/2026: Knip has an Expo plugin, takes `app/**` as the entry point
and reports "unused files, unused exports, unused dependencies, unused devDependencies,
unlisted dependencies" [Source: https://knip.dev/reference/plugins/expo]; Expo recommends
`jest-expo` and React Native Testing Library, with coverage through `collectCoverage` [Source:
https://docs.expo.dev/develop/unit-testing/]; Reassure measures "render characteristics,
duration and count", compared with the base branch in CI, running for both React Native and React web
[Source: https://github.com/callstack/reassure]; Flashlight gives "a performance score
for your app" on Android, iOS "in the works", able to run on real devices in CI
[Source: https://github.com/bamlab/flashlight]; StrykerJS mutation testing for Jest and
Vitest, with an incremental mode that runs only changed code [Source:
https://stryker-mutator.io/docs/stryker-js/introduction/]; Lighthouse CI runs on every
commit and fails the build when a budget is exceeded [Source: https://github.com/GoogleChrome/lighthouse-ci].
Performance thresholds of BRD version 4.5 section 17.1 (lines 1472 to 1474): the web screens Overview,
Focus, Board, WBS "Usable within 2 seconds at the 95th percentile, for projects up to
2,000 work items"; API reads under 1 second; saving under 1 second. D-26 (line 1650) takes these numbers
as defaults.

### 10.1 The rule: a line of code gets in only when a machine can prove that it is needed and correct

Every line of code must pass all five conditions, each condition being a machine gate:

1. **A test runs through it.** 100% line and branch coverage over the whole source code.
   Exclusions only through a list with a reason for each entry, for example the platform glue layer that can only be tested
   on a real device.
2. **That test really catches errors.** Mutation testing: the tool changes the code by itself (flipping a condition,
   deleting a statement), and the test must go red. High coverage with a test that asserts nothing fails here.
3. **Something uses it.** No file, export or dependency package is unused (Knip);
   no dictionary key is unread; no token in `brand/tokens.css`
   is unused unless it is on the debt list, which may only be shortened. Removing a feature
   forces these gates to remove its code, text and dependencies as well.
4. **If it is a control, it is in the screen contract** (the reverse check approved in section 8).
5. **Traceable to a requirement.** Every BRD requirement id that the screen contract declares must have at
   least one test carrying that id in its name; a missing one is red.

In addition, for beautiful and compact code: TypeScript in strict mode (unused variables and parameters
forbidden), ESLint with boundary rules for `core/` and the design system, a ceiling on function complexity and
a ceiling on file length, every disabling of a lint rule must state a reason, Prettier for formatting.

### 10.2 The suites

| Suite | Tool | What it measures | Cadence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Static checks | TypeScript, ESLint, Prettier | Types, rules, boundaries, formatting | Every commit |
| Dead code | Knip, the dictionary-key script, the token script | Unused files, exports, dependencies, keys, tokens | Every commit |
| Unit and component | Jest with `jest-expo`, React Native Testing Library | `core/` logic, components, screens; 100% coverage | Every commit |
| Data contract | zod | Mock data and mock server responses have the right shape | Every commit |
| Test quality | StrykerJS | Mutation score at or above the threshold fixed in the spec | Changed code on every pull request, everything nightly |
| Web E2E | Playwright on five platforms, axe-core | Behavior per the screen contract, layout against tokens, translation, brand, accessibility | Every pull request |
| Phone E2E | Maestro on the iOS Simulator and the Android Emulator | Behavior per the same screen contract, accessibility labels | Every pull request |
| Component performance | Reassure | Render time and count against the base branch | Every pull request |
| Web performance | Lighthouse CI | Budgets taken from BRD section 17.1 | Every pull request |
| Phone performance | Flashlight on Android | Performance score, frames, CPU, memory while running the Maestro flow | Nightly and before release, on a real device |
| Volume | Mock data of 2.000 items | The thresholds of BRD section 17.1 still hold when the project is large | Nightly |
| Visual | Screenshots of Playwright and Maestro | No deviation from the reference images after sign-off | Every pull request |
| Reverse tests | A script that breaks and then restores | Every gate knows how to report red | Nightly and when a gate changes |
| Dependencies | Vulnerability and license check of the packages | A package with a vulnerability or an invalid license | Nightly |

Reverse tests added for the new gates: add an export that nobody uses (Knip must go red);
add a function with no test (coverage must go red); delete an assertion in a test
(mutation testing must go red); add a heavy loop in a component (Reassure must go red);
add a large library to the web bundle (the web budget must go red); remove the requirement id from the test
name (the traceability gate must go red).

### 10.3 Ready for CI/CD

- Each gate is a command that can run on the developer's machine; CI only calls exactly that
  command again, and no logic lives only in a CI file.
- Three cadences: every commit runs the fast group (static checks, dead code, unit, data contract);
  every pull request runs everything (adding web and phone e2e, component and web performance,
  visual, mutation on changed code); nightly runs the slow group (full mutation, Flashlight
  on a real device, volume, reverse tests, dependencies).
- Two places to run: GitHub Actions for the web and common parts; Expo's EAS Workflows for
  the iOS and Android builds and the Maestro flow. Release later: EAS Build for the stores.

### 10.4 To be fixed in the spec, with proposals

- Mutation score threshold: proposed 90%, measure again after the first screen and only then fix it.
- Phone performance budget: the BRD has no number yet. Proposed: a cold app start under 2 seconds and
  scrolling holding 60 frames per second on a mid-range Android device; fix it after measuring the first screen.
- Ceilings on complexity and length: proposed cyclomatic complexity of at most 10 for a function, a file
  at most 300 lines.
- Where real devices are available to measure on (a cloud real-device service or devices in the office): not yet fixed.

### 10.5 Browser and device compliance (added per FE-14)

Sources, read on 05/10/2026:
- Playwright runs the branded Chrome through `channel: 'chrome'`, but "Playwright
  doesn't work with the branded version of Safari since it relies on patches"; phones
  in Playwright are only emulated. [Source: https://playwright.dev/docs/browsers]
- Real Safari can be driven with WebDriver through the `safaridriver` built into macOS;
  it runs on the iOS Simulator (`safari:useSimulator`) and on a real iPhone plugged into the
  Mac; each machine allows only one Safari session at a time. [Source: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/safari-developer-tools/webdriver ; https://webkit.org/blog/9395/webdriver-is-coming-to-safari-in-ios-13/]
- BrowserStack App Automate runs the Maestro flow on real iPhones and Android devices, called through
  REST API. [Source: https://www.browserstack.com/docs/app-automate/maestro/overview]
- `jest-expo/universal` "runs your tests with every Expo supported platform". [Source: https://github.com/expo/expo/tree/main/packages/jest-expo]
- eslint-plugin-compat reports when code uses a web API that the target browser does not support,
  according to the `browserslist` list. [Source: https://github.com/amilajack/eslint-plugin-compat]
- Expo SDK 57: the app runs from iOS 16.4 and Android 7. [Source: https://docs.expo.dev/versions/latest/]

Table of supported platforms (proposed, to be fixed in the spec):

| Tier | Platform | Version | Checked on every pull request | Checked nightly and before release |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Required | Chrome on desktop | The two latest major versions | Playwright, `chrome` channel | Same as the pull request |
| Required | Safari on macOS | The two latest major versions | Playwright WebKit, plus real Safari through `safaridriver` on a macOS machine | Same as the pull request |
| Required | Safari on iPhone | The two latest iOS versions | Safari on the iOS Simulator through `safaridriver` | Safari on a real iPhone |
| Required | Chrome on Android | The two latest versions | Playwright emulating a Pixel | Chrome on a real Android device |
| Required | iOS app | From iOS 16.4 | Maestro on the iOS Simulator | Maestro on a real iPhone |
| Required | Android app | From Android 7 | Maestro on the Android Emulator | Maestro and Flashlight on a real Android device |
| Supported, does not block merge | Edge, Firefox on desktop | The two latest major versions | None | Playwright `msedge` channel, Firefox |

"Well supported" means that the six gates of the screen are green on every platform of the required tier. Three more gates:

1. **Browser compliance at the code level:** `browserslist` lists exactly the web platforms in
   the table; eslint-plugin-compat turns lint red when the code uses a web API that a platform in the
   list does not support.
2. **Unit and component tests run on every platform** with `jest-expo/universal`
   (iOS, Android, web, Node).
3. **Real Safari runs a reduced e2e suite** that reads the same screen contract, with WebdriverIO and
   `safaridriver`, because Playwright cannot drive branded Safari.

Where no stable tool exists in the sources checked: automated performance measurement on iOS
(Flashlight for iOS "in the works"). For now measure with Xcode Instruments before every
release and record the numbers in the spec.

The column "checked nightly and before release" on real devices and browsers in the table above is
replaced by section 10.6: no paid real-device service; real devices are tested by a person; the part that needs
macOS runs on the developer's Mac before sending the pull request.

### 10.6 Where the suites run (per FE-15, replacing the where-to-run part of 10.3 and the real-device column of 10.5)

Sources, read on 05/10/2026:
- GitHub Actions "free for public repositories that use standard GitHub-hosted
  runners"; a private repo on the Free plan gets 2.000 minutes per month; price per minute: Linux 2
  cores $0.006, macOS $0.062; 500 MB artifact storage, 10 GB cache. [Source: https://docs.github.com/en/billing/concepts/product-billing/github-actions]
- Since 02/04/2024, the 2-core Linux machines of GitHub Actions have hardware acceleration for the Android
  Emulator, and KVM must be enabled in the workflow. [Source: https://github.blog/changelog/2024-04-02-github-actions-hardware-accelerated-android-virtualization-now-available/ ; https://github.com/marketplace/actions/android-emulator-runner]

Three places to run:

1. **Free CI: GitHub Actions on Linux machines.** Runs everything that does not need macOS:
   - static checks, dead code, browser compatibility in the code, unit and component tests on
     four platforms (`jest-expo/universal`), the data contract, mutation testing on changed code;
   - web e2e with Playwright on Chrome, Edge, Firefox, WebKit, an emulated Pixel and
     iPhone, with axe-core, layout measurement, translation, brand, screenshot comparison;
   - Lighthouse CI, Reassure, the volume tests;
   - the Android app on the Android Emulator with Maestro;
   - reverse tests and the dependency vulnerability check on a schedule.
   No macOS machine in CI, no EAS Workflows, no paid real-device service.
   If the repo is private, the scheduled suites are paced so that the total time stays
   within 2.000 minutes per month; any suite that does not fit runs only in the command of item 2.
2. **The developer's Mac: one command before sending a pull request.** Proposed name
   `pnpm verify`. The command runs everything CI runs, plus the part that can only run on macOS:
   - real Safari on macOS and Safari on the iOS Simulator, with WebdriverIO and
     `safaridriver` (one Safari session per machine at a time, so they run one after another);
   - build the iOS app with Xcode and run the Maestro flow on the iOS Simulator.
   It ends with a report, one green or red line per gate, with the commit id, and exits
   with a code other than 0 if any gate is red. Optional, switched on with a flag: the command attaches the status "checked
   on macOS" to exactly that commit on GitHub, so that a branch protection rule demands this
   status before merge; when the commit changes, the status no longer applies.
3. **A person testing on real devices, before every release**, following a checklist kept
   in the repo: which device, which flow (taken from the screen contract), reading the screen with VoiceOver and
   TalkBack, measuring performance with Xcode Instruments on iPhone and Flashlight on an Android
   device plugged into the computer. The results are recorded in a file per date.

Removed from the design: BrowserStack and every paid real-device service; EAS Workflows in CI.
The remaining tools are all open source or available free of charge [Unverified - the spec records the license
of each package after checking].
